description: TechNest Thinkers is building Outpost Commander, a browser mission trainer for kids aged 7-12. Players run a small astronaut base on the Moon, then Mars, balancing power, life support and radiation safety. Every choice has a trade-off, and real NASA data (DONKI solar flares, RadLab ISS radiation) drives each day’s events. A tutorial, Mars communication delay, ranks and NASA science cards turn play into training. Seeking game/web developers and designers.
summary: Survive the Sol is a free browser game that trains kids aged 7–12 to think like astronauts. Players command a small base on the Moon and must keep their crew safe for 12 days by managing three real mission resources: Power, Life Support and Radiation Safety. Each day they pick three Emergency Cards, explore a 3D lunar surface to collect supplies, and then face a solar storm taken from real NASA CCMC DONKI solar flare records, shown on screen with its real class and date. Using the right card at the right moment, such as a Radiation Shield, a Water Wall or the Storm Shelter, protects the crew, while every choice has a real cost. A night report explains what happened and shares a real space-science fact from NASA OSDR. Radiation damage is scaled with RadLab ISS dose data. Mars adds dust storms and a communication delay with Earth, so players must decide on their own. The game teaches power budgeting, radiation shielding, life support and decision-making through play, needs no login or install, and works on laptops and phones.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Survive the Sol is a free 3D browser game for kids aged 7–12, built for the challenge "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer". Players learn the real trade-offs astronauts face by keeping a small Moon base safe for 12 days.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Name page and lobby – no login and no personal data. The commander name is stored only on the player's own device.

2. Each day the player picks 3 of 5 Emergency Cards (such as Radiation Shield, Water Wall, Storm Shelter, Duck & Cover and Power Save). Every card shows its benefit, its cost and a "Real science" line.

3. The player explores the Moon in third person and collects glowing supplies: ice for Life Support, solar panels for Power and shield plates for Radiation Safety.

4. A solar storm hits. The flare is a real event from NASA CCMC DONKI and is shown on screen with its real class, date and source (for example, "C1.0 solar flare · 31 August 2026 · Source: NASA CCMC DONKI · archived NASA data"). The player must use the right card or stay inside the safe zone around the base. The right card gives full protection, a wrong card gives less, and ROVI the robot helper explains why.

5. A night report shows the bars before and after, how much the card saved, 1–3 stars, and a "Did you know?" fact from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (RadLab).

6. Storms get stronger over the 12 days, moving from small C-class flares to bigger M- and X-class flares.

WHAT KIDS LEARN

- Power budgeting: energy is limited and every action costs something

- Radiation shielding: how soil, water and shelters protect astronauts during solar storms

- Life support: why air, water and food matter in space

- Decision-making under pressure, the way real crews must act

WHY IT MATTERS

Real NASA space-weather data becomes decisions kids can feel. The game is free, needs no install or login, and can be shared with one link by teachers and parents. It runs in any modern browser on laptops and phones.

TOOLS USED

HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Three.js for 3D graphics; Python scripts to fetch and save NASA data; Web Audio for sound; GitHub for code and hosting.

DESIGN CHOICES

Only three core resources, a cost on every choice, simple English, no violence, tooltips for hard words (sol, solar flare, radiation dose, regolith), and all stored data is clearly labelled "archived NASA data".
